title: Pheasants
body: Pheasants are shy, charming birds known for their brilliant plumage. They belong to the order Galliformes, known as game birds, and the family Phasinidae. There are 51 species of pheasants in the world, shown in an identification chart brought out by the Environment Society of India (ESI) to create awareness among school eco-clubs under the National Green Corps (NGC). Except for the Congo Peafowl, all pheasants are from Asia. Scientists believe that pheasants originated in the Himalayas and then scattered into Tibet, China, Myanmar and South and South East Asia. About a third of all the pheasants in the world are found in India. The peacock, the best known member of the family, is India's national bird and has a prominent place in Indian art, culture and folklore. (Adapted from the passage used in the chapter.)

title: Coal and petroleum
body: The energy stored in coal and petroleum originally came to the earth from the sun. The bulk of present-day supplies was laid down some 200 to 600 million years ago, when tropical conditions were widespread and swampy forests and warm coastal seas teemed with life. When these organisms died, much of their tissue was recycled through scavenging and decay, but a significant amount was covered with mud, which prevented complete decomposition. Over time, layers of fine sediment were deposited and their weight turned the sediments to rock. Sandwiched between the layers, coal and petroleum were produced and preserved under pressure. Coal may still be forming here and there, but conditions today are not right for producing it in significant quantities. (Adapted from the passage used in the chapter.)
